details:
**Jason and the Golden Fleece**
Medea is a sorceress princess of Colchis, daughter of King Aeetes, granddaughter of the sun god Helios, and a priestess of Hecate. When Jason and the Argonauts come for the Golden Fleece, she falls in love with him and uses her magic to help him win it. In Pindar's Fourth Pythian Ode, Aphrodite gives Jason the iynx, a wryneck bird tied to a spinning wheel, as a love charm to win Medea.

**Poisoned robe for Glauce**
When Jason abandons Medea in Corinth to marry Glauce (also called Creusa), daughter of King Creon, Medea sends the bride a poisoned robe and golden crown. When Glauce puts them on, she bursts into flames, and Creon dies too when he embraces his daughter's body.

**Killing her own children**
Medea's ultimate revenge on Jason is murdering their sons, named Mermeros and Pheres in some sources. In other versions the Corinthians kill the children. Hera is sometimes said to have made the children immortal.

**Euripides's Medea**
The famous 431 BCE tragedy. Creon banishes Medea from Corinth because he fears her, she gives a celebrated speech on the miserable lot of women and of a foreign "barbarian" bride, and Jason sneers that women only care about whether "everything is fine in bed" and wishes there were no female sex. It ends with the murders of Glauce, Creon, and her children.

**Dragon chariot of Helios**
At the end of Euripides's play Medea escapes Corinth with her children's bodies in a flying chariot drawn by dragons (serpents), sent by her grandfather Helios, and flies toward Athens.

**Absyrtus (Apsyrtus)**
Medea's brother (or half-brother). To slow her father's pursuit of the fleeing Argo, she chops him to pieces and scatters the parts so Aeetes must stop to gather them; in Apollonius of Rhodes's Argonautica she lures him into an ambush where Jason kills him. Circe later purifies them of the murder, and the islands named for him, the Absyrtides, were said to be cleared of snakes that Medea confined in his tomb.

**Pelias's daughters and the ram**
To avenge Jason on his usurping uncle King Pelias of Iolcus, Medea chops up an old ram and boils it in a cauldron, and it jumps out as a young lamb. Convinced, Pelias's daughters cut up and boil their own father, but she gives them no magic and he stays dead. In one version she disguises herself as a priestess of Artemis to win access to the palace.

**Aegeus and the wineskin oracle**
In Euripides's play King Aegeus of Athens passes through Corinth on his way to King Pittheus of Troezen, puzzling over an oracle telling him not to "unstop the wineskin's neck" (or "foot") until he gets home. Medea promises to cure his childlessness with drugs in exchange for refuge in Athens, and she later marries him.

**Attempting to poison Theseus**
In Athens Medea recognizes Aegeus's long-lost son Theseus and tries to have him poisoned at a feast. Aegeus recognizes his son's sword just in time, knocks the cup away, and drives Medea out of Athens.

**Talos**
The bronze giant who guards Crete by throwing boulders at ships. His life depends on a single vein sealed at the ankle by a bronze nail. Medea bewitches him by summoning the Keres (death spirits) with her evil eye, and in Apollodorus she removes the nail so his ichor drains out and he dies.

**Fire-breathing bulls and the dragon's teeth**
Aeetes demands that Jason yoke a pair of bronze-footed, fire-breathing bulls and sow dragon's teeth, which sprout into armed warriors. Medea gives Jason a protective ointment and advises him to throw a stone into the crowd of warriors so they fight one another.

**The Promethean ointment**
The ointment she gives Jason comes from a crocus-like flower that grew from the ichor dripping from Prometheus's wounds in the Caucasus. She carries its juice in a shell, and it makes the wearer invulnerable to bronze and fire for one day.

**Rejuvenating Aeson**
In Ovid's Metamorphoses Medea restores youth to Jason's aged father Aeson by draining his blood and replacing it with a magic potion she brews from herbs. In the same work she draws the moon down from the sky for her witchcraft.

**Wedding in the cave of Macris**
While the Argonauts flee the Colchians, King Alcinous of the Phaeacians rules that he will hand Medea back only if she is still a virgin. Medea and Jason hurriedly marry in the sacred cave of Macris on the island of Drepane (Scheria) so that she can stay with him.

**Later life and adaptations**
In later myth Medea returns to Colchis and helps depose her uncle Perses, who had usurped Aeetes's throne, and some sources say she married Achilles in the Isles of the Blessed after her death. Her story was retold in Seneca's Latin tragedy Medea and in a 20th-century adaptation by the poet Robinson Jeffers.
